findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make AGENTS.md, docs/orphaned-processes.md and `is_rebar_detached_worker` use one identical recognition rule (the `import <module>; <module>.<func>(` shape for all three modules), and test that the documented strings match the detector's pattern.
evidence: "recognise them by a command line containing `import rebar._commands.compact_trigger`, `rebar._snapshot.gc_trigger` or `rebar._store.push`"
"add `is_rebar_detached_worker(command)` matching the `spawn_detached` command shape (`import <module>; <module>.<func>(`)"
"neither is a command that merely mentions `rebar` in an argument"
findings.finding: The plan gives three different recognition rules for the same workers. AGENTS.md uses loose substrings that are not even parallel: `import rebar._commands.compact_trigger` carries an `import ` prefix, while `rebar._snapshot.gc_trigger` and `rebar._store.push` do not. The detector uses the strict shape `import <module>; <module>.<func>(`. The tests require that 'a command that merely mentions rebar in an argument' is NOT recognised, yet the AGENTS.md substring `rebar._store.push` would match exactly such a mention (e.g. `pytest tests/... -k rebar._store.push`). This also conflicts with the AC that the two documents 'agree'.
findings.location: Approach step 1 vs Approach step 3 vs Testing (Detector)
scenarios: An agent-started `python -m pytest ... rebar._store.push` helper stuck at PPID 1 is treated as exempt by an agent following AGENTS.md, while the detector correctly does not label it.
findings.suggested_fix: In AGENTS.md, phrase all three uniformly as `import rebar._commands.compact_trigger; rebar._commands.compact_trigger.`, `import rebar._snapshot.gc_trigger; ...` and `import rebar._store.push; ...` (or say 'a `python -c` command beginning `import <module>; <module>.`'). Add a guidance-test assertion that each documented example string satisfies `is_rebar_detached_worker`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make AGENTS.md (and docs/orphaned-processes.md) identify workers by the same full `import <module>; <module>.<func>(` shape the detector matches, naming the three module/function pairs, and have the guidance test pin both module and function.

findings.finding: AGENTS.md's identification rule is looser than the detector's matcher. It accepts any command line 'containing … `rebar._snapshot.gc_trigger` or `rebar._store.push`' (two of the three patterns have no `import` prefix and no function name). The detector instead requires the `import <module>; <module>.<func>(` shape. The carve-out is meant to cover only processes rebar detaches, 'not ones the agent starts', but an agent's own helper (e.g. `python -c "from rebar._store.push import …"` in a loop, or a pytest run naming that module) matches the AGENTS.md substring and would be left running at PPID 1. That reopens the agent-helper leak the rule exists to prevent.
scenarios: An agent starts `python -c 'import rebar._store.push as p; while True: p…'`, orphans it, and AGENTS.md's substring rule tells the next session it is exempt.

It passes for a doc that says nothing at all, so Acceptance criterion 3 (doc says safe to interrupt, SIGTERM preferred) has no positive check and no link to `_INTERRUPTIBLE_REMEDIES`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reword the detector's rebar-worker note so a flagged worker over the CPU threshold is described as abnormal (e.g. 'rebar detached worker over threshold — likely stuck; SIGTERM it, and file a bug'), and make the footer not apply investigation-owner advice to rebar-worker lines.

scripts/check_orphaned_load.py _report footer text about the 'owning investigation'
Context: the observed sweep 'exited on its own within about a minute'
findings.finding: The detector only flags records above DEFAULT_MIN_CPU_SECONDS (3600 CPU-seconds). So every rebar worker it labels has, by definition, behaved abnormally: the plan itself expects a sweep to end within about a minute and calls one over the threshold 'a runaway worker'. Attaching 'exits on its own' to exactly those records sends the wrong message, and it sits next to the existing footer ('Confirm the owning investigation is over, then terminate only the specific pids…'), which assumes an agent-started helper. The report gives the operator contradictory advice for the one case where it matters.
scenarios: A sweep stuck in a loop has used 2h of CPU. The report says it 'exits on its own', so the agent leaves it running indefinitely.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] For each of the three spawn sites, state the exact detached child argv (module + function as it appears in `ps`), and make the guidance test pin the module/function passed into the spawned command rather than the caller's module.

findings.finding: The guidance test pins the 'module of each `spawn_detached` caller', but the detector and docs key on the worker module/function that appears in the spawned command line. These are not necessarily the same. For the async push, the plan names `rebar._store.push.push_tickets_branch`, which reads like the spawning function rather than the detached entry point. The detached child might be a different function, or even a bare `git push` with no `import rebar...` in its argv. Whether each spawn site actually produces a `python -c 'import <module>; <module>.<func>(...)'` command line is load-bearing and is not stated.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify how the guidance test enumerates `spawn_detached` call sites (e.g. an AST walk over src/rebar extracting the module argument), and assert the discovered set has exactly 3 members so a silent zero-match fails.
evidence: "The test pins them against the module paths passed to `spawn_detached` in src/rebar, so a new spawn site without guidance fails it."
findings.finding: The mechanism by which the guidance test discovers 'the module paths passed to `spawn_detached` in src/rebar' is unspecified. It could be an AST scan of call sites, a grep for string literals, or a hardcoded list. If modules are passed as variables or built dynamically, a naive grep will silently find nothing and the 'new spawn site fails it' guarantee is void. The plan also does not say the discovery result should be checked for cardinality.
scenarios: The scan regex misses the spawn_detached call shape, returns an empty set, and the test passes vacuously.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Confirm (citing the push/GC code or a timeout) that the async push and GC have a bounded runtime, or add guidance such as 'a rebar worker at PPID 1 older than N minutes is not expected; investigate'.
evidence: "These workers end on their own: the async push and GC are one-shot"
"It is still reported when over the CPU threshold"
"leave them to finish"
findings.finding: The claim that 'these workers end on their own' is asserted for the async push and GC without validation. A push is network-bound and can hang on a stalled remote or a credential prompt. Such a hang uses near-zero CPU, so the CPU-threshold detector never surfaces it. Meanwhile the guidance tells agents to 'leave them to finish', so a hung push could sit at PPID 1 indefinitely and be deliberately ignored.
findings.location: Decision: the guidance is wrong, not the code; Approach steps 1-3
scenarios: `git push` blocks on a network stall for hours at PPID 1 with 0% CPU. It is never flagged, and agents are told to leave it alone.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the default explicitly: recognition only adds a label, and flagging criteria and exit status are unchanged for recognised workers.
evidence: "When a flagged record matches, its report line carries a 'rebar detached worker' label"
"It is still reported when over the CPU threshold"
findings.finding: The detector's behaviour for recognised workers below the CPU threshold, and its exit status, are implicit. 'It is still reported when over the CPU threshold' could mean the detector already reports only over-threshold PPID 1 records. It could also mean recognised workers under the threshold are now suppressed. The plan also does not say whether a labelled over-threshold worker still yields the same non-zero/flagged exit.
scenarios: The implementer adds suppression for under-threshold workers, or changes the exit code for labelled ones, without the author intending it.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: 'Recognition changes only the report text; which records are flagged and the script's exit status are unchanged.'

"It is still reported when over the CPU threshold, because a runaway worker is a real problem."
The plan states no timeout or maximum lifetime for push_tickets_branch or gc_trigger
findings.finding: The guidance tells agents to 'leave them to finish' because the workers 'exit on its own', but nothing bounds how long that takes. A detached tickets-branch push blocked on the network or remote makes no CPU progress. Because the detector only flags records over the CPU threshold, a hung push is never reported, and the carve-out tells agents to leave it alone indefinitely.
findings.location: Decision section ('These workers end on their own: the async push and GC are one-shot') and Approach step 3
scenarios: A push stalls on an unreachable remote and sits at PPID 1 for hours. It is below the CPU threshold, so the detector stays silent, and AGENTS.md says it is exempt, so no agent ever reaps it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Scope the ps/SIGTERM recipe in docs/orphaned-processes.md to POSIX explicitly, and add the Windows equivalent: identify by command line (e.g. via Get-CimInstance Win32_Process CommandLine) and note that termination there is immediate, not at a ticket boundary.
evidence: "how to identify each from `ps -o pid=,ppid=,command=`"
"SIGTERM is preferred because it ends the sweep at a ticket boundary"
Plan context: spawn_detached uses `DETACHED_PROCESS` on Windows
Python on Windows: os.kill with SIGTERM calls TerminateProcess; no handler runs
findings.finding: The identification and stop recipe assumes POSIX. The doc tells agents to identify workers via `ps -o pid=,ppid=,command=` and to stop a sweep with SIGTERM 'because it ends the sweep at a ticket boundary'. On Windows, spawn_detached uses DETACHED_PROCESS: there is no POSIX `ps` with `-o`, there is no PPID 1 reparenting, and `os.kill(pid, SIGTERM)` maps to TerminateProcess. That hard-kills the worker without running install_stop_on_sigterm's ticket-boundary stop, so the documented recipe is false there.
findings.location: Approach step 2 (docs/orphaned-processes.md: 'how to identify each from `ps -o pid=,ppid=,command=`' and 'SIGTERM is preferred because it ends the sweep at a ticket boundary')
scenarios: Windows developer workstation: an agent runs the documented `ps -o pid=,ppid=,command=` and gets an error. PowerShell's `ps` alias for Get-Process rejects `-o`, and cmd has no ps, so the agent cannot identify the worker as documented.
Windows: an agent 'SIGTERMs' a blocking sweep per the doc. The process is terminated immediately rather than at a ticket boundary, contrary to the guidance.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a 'Windows' note: workers are DETACHED_PROCESS and never show PPID 1. Identify them with `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object CommandLine -like '*import rebar._*'`. Stop-Process/TerminateProcess skips the ticket-boundary handler; the sweep remains safe to interrupt because events stay live.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that is_rebar_detached_worker takes precedence over is_default_suppressed (a recognised worker is never system-suppressed), and add a test whose worker command line starts with /usr/bin/python3.
evidence: Plan: 'It is still reported when over the CPU threshold, because a runaway worker is a real problem.'
scripts/check_orphaned_load.py: `and (include_system or not is_default_suppressed(record.command))`; _SYSTEM_PATH_PREFIXES includes '/usr/bin/'
src/rebar/_proc.py spawn_detached: argv[0] is `sys.executable`
findings.finding: The plan says a recognised rebar worker 'is still reported when over the CPU threshold'. But find_orphaned_load drops any record whose command line starts with a system path (is_default_suppressed checks /usr/bin/ and others) before any new recognition would run. spawn_detached starts the child with sys.executable, so a worker under /usr/bin/python3 (system Python on Linux, Xcode CLT Python on macOS) is suppressed by default. It is never labelled or reported unless the user passes --include-system.
scenarios: rebar installed into system Python on Linux: a runaway sweep under /usr/bin/python3 at PPID 1 burns CPU for hours, and check_orphaned_load reports it only as '1 launchd/init-owned suppressed'.
findings.suggested_fix: In find_orphaned_load, change the suppression clause to `(include_system or is_rebar_detached_worker(record.command) or not is_default_suppressed(record.command))`, and add a detector test with a `/usr/bin/python3 -c "import sys; ...; import rebar._commands.compact_trigger; rebar._commands.compact_trigger.run_detached_sweep(...)"` record over the threshold.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Build the detector test records from the same code path spawn_detached uses to form its argv (or assert against a shared constant/helper), so a change to the spawned command shape breaks the test.
evidence: "a record carrying the real `spawn_detached` command line for each of the three entry points is recognised"
"matching the `spawn_detached` command shape (`import <module>; <module>.<func>(`)"
findings.finding: The detector tests use a 'real `spawn_detached` command line', but the plan does not say whether it is produced by spawn_detached's own command construction or hand-copied into the test. If hand-written, the matcher and its test share one self-authored oracle. A later change to how spawn_detached formats the `-c` payload (spacing, quoting, a different separator) would make is_rebar_detached_worker stop matching real workers while the tests stay green.
scenarios: spawn_detached is changed to emit `import mod;mod.func(` (no space). Real workers lose the label in reports, and the hand-copied test strings still match.
